# Concurrency Fundamentals

A process is an operating-system container for a running program. Each JVM
started from this JAR is a separate process with its own heap and resources. A
thread is an execution path inside one process; threads in that process share
its memory and resources.

Each process has its own virtual address space. Memory allocated to the first
JVM belongs to the first process; the second JVM cannot directly read or modify
it, even though both run the same JAR. Processes must use an explicit mechanism,
such as a socket, a file, or shared memory, to exchange data.

Threads in one process execute in that same address space, so they can share the
process heap and the objects stored there. Each thread has its own call stack.
In Java, sharing an address space does not bypass reference reachability or
language access rules, but a mutable object shared between threads still needs
coordination to avoid races and visibility problems.

```text
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Operating system                                                                           │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │ JVM process                             │  │ JVM process                             │  │
│  │  ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐       │  │  ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐       │  │
│  │  │ Thread │ │ Thread │ │ Thread │       │  │  │ Thread │ │ Thread │ │ Thread │       │  │
│  │  └────────┘ └────────┘ └────────┘       │  │  └────────┘ └────────┘ └────────┘       │  │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────┘  └─────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

The diagram shows two processes. Starting the JAR twice creates two such
process-and-thread groups under the operating system.

All Java application code executes in a thread; a process supplies the resources
and isolation boundary, rather than executing code itself. The JVM normally
remains alive while at least one non-daemon thread is running. When the last
non-daemon thread finishes, the JVM starts normal shutdown and the application
exits. Daemon threads do not keep the JVM alive and may be stopped at shutdown.
`System.exit`, `Runtime.halt`, a crash, or the operating system can end a
process by a different path.

This is an introductory observation exercise. It establishes the distinction
between processes and threads before later examples create and coordinate
application threads.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this example, attendees can:

- distinguish a JVM process from the threads executing within it;
- explain why separate processes do not directly share memory; and
- use `jcmd` to list JVM processes and inspect a process’s threads.

## Prerequisite

- [Oracle Java 8](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/#java8)

## The program to inspect

The program keeps its non-daemon `main` thread asleep for an intentionally
impractical duration, leaving a JVM process available for inspection. It is not
an interruption example: an interrupt would end the sleep and let `main` exit,
but neither `jcmd` nor the `kill` command used here performs a Java
`Thread.interrupt()`. Starting the JAR twice creates two independent JVM
processes that we can inspect.

```java
package demo;

public final class Main {

    public static void main(final String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        System.out.println("Ready for inspection");
        Thread.sleep(Long.MAX_VALUE);
    }

    private Main() {}
}
```

## References

- [The `Thread` class (Java SE 8)](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/lang/Thread.html)
- [JVM Specification, §2.5: Run-Time Data Areas (Java SE 8)](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jvms/se8/html/jvms-2.html#jvms-2.5)

## Guided walkthrough

Run these commands from this example directory.

1. Build the application JAR.

   ```shell
   ./mvnw clean package
   ```

2. Start two copies of the application in the background. Each command creates a
   separate JVM process. Each process remains available for inspection while its
   `main` thread sleeps; its output is redirected to files so the commands can
   finish. Save both process IDs for the inspection commands below.

   Start the first process

   ```shell
   java -jar './target/libs/fundamentals-1.0.0.jar' > './target/first.log' 2>&1 &

   # Save the PID so later steps can reuse it after this entry finishes.
   echo "$!" > './target/first.pid'
   ```

   Start the second process.

   ```shell
   java -jar './target/libs/fundamentals-1.0.0.jar' > './target/second.log' 2>&1 &

   # Save the PID so later steps can reuse it after this entry finishes.
   echo "$!" > './target/second.pid'
   ```

3. List the Java processes. The JAR appears twice: once for each process started
   above.

   ```shell
   jcmd -l
   ```

   The Java processes on this machine

   ```
   119905 ./target/libs/fundamentals-1.0.0.jar
   119961 sun.tools.jcmd.JCmd -l
   119948 ./target/libs/fundamentals-1.0.0.jar
   ```

   `jcmd -l` lists discoverable JVM processes together with their process IDs
   and launch information. Locate the two `fundamentals-1.0.0.jar` entries;
   their PIDs should match the values saved in `first.pid` and `second.pid`. The
   next command uses the first PID to request a thread dump from that specific
   JVM process.

4. Print the thread dump for the first process. It includes the waiting `main`
   thread and JVM service threads. Run the same command with `second.pid` to
   inspect the independent thread set in the other process.

   ```shell
   jcmd "$(cat './target/first.pid')" Thread.print
   ```

   This will show the target process’s threads, such as main and JVM service
   threads, along with their states and stack traces. It may also show lock
   information, which helps diagnose blocked or waiting threads.

   ```

      java.lang.Thread.State: RUNNABLE
   ```

   Thread-dump contents are implementation- and configuration-dependent. Locate
   the application’s main thread and inspect its stack; while this program is
   sleeping, it will usually show `Thread.sleep`. The remaining JVM service
   threads and their states are not a stable teaching target.

5. Stop the two background JVM processes after the inspection. The PID files
   identify only the processes started in this walkthrough. `kill` sends a
   process-termination signal; it does not invoke `Thread.interrupt()` on
   `main`.

   ```shell
   kill "$(cat './target/first.pid')"  2>/dev/null
   kill "$(cat './target/second.pid')" 2>/dev/null
   ```
